blockMcqs.question: Why must systems eventually scale horizontally instead of just vertically?
options: Horizontal scaling never needs a load balancer
One machine has a hard capacity ceiling
Vertical scaling requires rewriting the app
Horizontal scaling is always cheaper
blockMcqs.explanation: A single box maxes out on CPU, RAM, and disk, forcing more machines.

blockMcqs.question: Batching requests together typically does what?
options: Lowers latency and throughput together
Raises throughput but raises per-request latency
Lowers throughput but lowers latency
Has no effect on either metric
blockMcqs.explanation: Less per-item overhead lifts throughput, but each item waits for the batch.

blockMcqs.question: A feature needs two services each at 99.9%. Its availability is about:
options: 99.9%, the same as each
99.99%, redundancy improves it
99.8%, series dependencies multiply
100%, the services back each other up
blockMcqs.explanation: Needing both means 0.999 x 0.999, which is worse than either alone.

blockMcqs.question: Why is statelessness the precondition for horizontal scaling?
options: It removes the need for any database
It makes each request faster to process
Any node can serve any request and be killed freely
It guarantees strong consistency across nodes
blockMcqs.explanation: With no local per-client state, the LB routes anywhere and nodes are disposable.

blockMcqs.question: Why can't a real distributed system simply "choose CA"?
options: Consistency and availability are the same property
Partitions are unavoidable, so P is mandatory
CA systems are too expensive to operate
Availability always implies consistency
blockMcqs.explanation: Networks will partition, leaving only a C-versus-A choice during one.

blockMcqs.question: In the standard stack, what holds the durable source of truth?
options: The cache
The CDN
The database
The load balancer
blockMcqs.explanation: Caches and CDNs are fast copies; the database is the authoritative store.

blockMcqs.question: Read traffic is 100x your writes. Best first scaling move?
options: Shard the write path immediately
Cache the hot set, then add read replicas
Switch the whole system to strong consistency
Replace the database with an object store
blockMcqs.explanation: Caching absorbs the hot reads; replicas spread the rest off the primary.

blockMcqs.question: Postgres read replicas scale reads but introduce what cost?
options: Replication lag, so reads can be stale
Loss of all write durability
Mandatory strong consistency on every read
A single point of failure on the primary
blockMcqs.explanation: Async copying means a replica trails the primary by milliseconds to seconds.
